extracted.intended_audience: physicians, clinical researchers and other professionals who review manuscripts for The BMJ
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for clinicians and researchers who are asked to review manuscripts submitted to The BMJ, covering procedural requirements, expectations about what to prioritise, and how reports are handled under BMJ's open peer review policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open (signed) peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: The BMJ uses open peer review: reviewers have to sign their reports, saying briefly who they are and where they work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When signing, identify yourself and your affiliation in the report. Be aware that open peer review means your name will be associated with the report; if you experience any adverse event arising from open peer review or want to comment on it, email papersadmin@bmj.com.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration of competing interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are asked to declare to the editors any competing interests that might relate to articles we have asked them to review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose any financial, professional, or personal conflicts that could bias your review. Use the editors' guidance (see BMJ transparency policy) if unsure what constitutes a competing interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: No direct contact with authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Open peer review does not mean that authors should feel able to contact reviewers directly to discuss their reports; all queries should still be directed through the editorial office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an author wishes to respond or discuss, direct them to the editorial office. Maintain professional boundaries and route communications via the journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to review invitations via the online editorial office
rubrics_metrics.description: If the BMJ needs your help appraising a manuscript they will email you and ask you to accept or reject the reviewing invitation at their online editorial office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept or decline promptly through the journal's system so editors can find alternative reviewers if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise manuscripts according to BMJ's aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should help prioritise manuscripts bearing in mind that the BMJ aims to publish original, important, and reliable articles that will help readers (mainly doctors) make better decisions about practice, policy, education, and research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a manuscript, explicitly consider originality, importance, reliability (rigour), and clinical or policy relevance. Use these priorities to advise editors about suitability for The BMJ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advise editors; editors make the final decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers advise the editors, who are responsible for the final decision to accept or reject a manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame your report to provide clear, evidence-based recommendations and commentary for editors. Understand that editors synthesise reviewer input and have ultimate responsibility for decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware reviewers' reports may be shared within BMJ Group
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors can nominate other BMJ Journals to transfer their manuscript and the system also passes on editors' comments and peer reviewers' reports; a review provided for The BMJ may be seen later by other editors within the BMJ Group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write reports knowing they may be reused or seen by other BMJ journals' editors. Ensure professionalism, completeness, and appropriate confidentiality when composing your review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers can access each other's reports after decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts sent for review are usually seen by at least two reviewers, and reviewers can access each other's reports on the same manuscript once The BMJ has made its decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate that your report may be visible to other reviewers post-decision; avoid inappropriate language and provide constructive, well-evidenced critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raise ethical concerns via BMJ transparency policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The BMJ transparency policy pulls together advice on what to do if you are concerned about the ethics aspects of a manuscript or suspect plagiarism, duplicate publication, or scientific fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you detect ethical problems, plagiarism, duplicate publication, or suspected fraud, follow the steps in the BMJ transparency policy and contact the editors rather than confronting authors directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer recognition and record-keeping
rubrics_metrics.description: To thank reviewers The BMJ offers a year’s online subscription to bmj.com and provides reviewers with a Journal Activity Certificate that tracks reviewing activity for CPD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Journal Activity Certificate to document reviews for continuing professional development. If you already have access to bmj.com and wish to transfer the subscription, consider passing it to a colleague.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide feedback on the review process
rubrics_metrics.description: The BMJ welcomes feedback from reviewers about manuscripts reviewed and about the BMJ review process in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have comments about a specific decision or the peer review process, contact the journal to share constructive feedback; the BMJ also conducts editorial research and training based on reviewer input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand article provenance statements
rubrics_metrics.description: At the end of every accepted editorial, research article, clinical review, practice article, analysis, feature, and head-to-head article The BMJ will add a statement explaining the article's provenance (e.g. 'Not commissioned; externally peer reviewed', 'Commissioned; not externally peer reviewed').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that accepted articles carry provenance labels that indicate whether they were externally peer reviewed, commissioned, or both; this transparency relates directly to reviewers' contributions.
